title: Supervision 1 short-answer questions
description: Five short-answer questions (SAQs) on this week’s lectures. They’re for practice, not to hand in.
instructions:
Optional practice. These short-answer questions go with this week’s lectures. Only the essay needs to be handed in, but SAQs are good practice at writing short, focused answers, and they’re good revision too.

  • There’s no time limit, but about 10 minutes for each is a good aim.
  • Answer as many as you like. You can leave some blank and still submit.
  • After you submit, Review my answers shows you the points a good answer covers.

questions.title: Feedforward, negative feedback and thirst
questions.text: Define ‘feedforward’ and ‘negative feedback’, and explain how these processes relate to thirst.
questions.guidance:
• Negative feedback. A sensor detects a change in a regulated variable, a comparator compares the variable with its set point, and the error signal drives an effector response that opposes the change.
  • Feedforward. A response is set going in anticipation of a change, or as soon as its cause is detected, before an error signal appears in the regulated variable.
  • Thirst as negative feedback. Water loss (through sweating, for example) raises plasma osmolarity. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, in areas without a blood–brain barrier, trigger thirst and the release of ADH, and drinking and water retention bring the osmolarity back down.
  • The problem of the delay. Water takes time to be absorbed from the gut. If we kept drinking until our osmolarity was back to normal, we’d drink too much and overshoot, because negative feedback with a delay oscillates.
  • Thirst as feedforward. Receptors in the mouth, throat and stomach signal that water has been drunk, and they switch thirst off before the water is absorbed. Dogs with oesophageal fistulae (Bellows, 1938) drank about the right amount and stopped, then started again later, because the water never reached the gut. Drinking with meals is anticipatory too.

questions.title: Crossing cell membranes
questions.text: What are the ways in which solutes can cross cell membranes, and how do they differ?
questions.guidance:
• Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer is for small, non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂, steroids). It’s passive and goes down the concentration gradient, with no protein involved. It isn’t saturable, and its rate depends on the gradient and on how lipid-soluble the molecule is.
  • Channels are passive too, and very fast. Ion channels let ions move down their electrochemical gradient, and they’re selective and often gated, by voltage, ligands or stretch. Aquaporins are channels for water.
  • Facilitated diffusion carriers (such as the GLUT glucose transporters) are also passive. A change in the carrier’s shape moves the solute across. They’re specific and saturable (they have a maximum rate), and slower than channels.
  • Primary active transport (such as the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and the Ca²⁺-ATPases) uses ATP directly to move solutes against their gradients.
  • Secondary active transport uses the energy stored in another solute’s gradient, usually the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. It includes symporters (the Na⁺–glucose transporter, SGLT) and antiporters (the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ and Na⁺/H⁺ exchangers).
  • Vesicles carry large molecules, by endocytosis, exocytosis (as in the release of water-soluble hormones) and transcytosis.
  • A good answer compares them: the energy each one uses, its direction relative to the gradient, how specific it is, whether it saturates, how fast it is, and how it’s regulated.

questions.title: Designing an experiment on a hormone
questions.text: What are the theoretical problems that you might encounter in designing and interpreting an experiment to investigate the effects of a hormone on the body?
questions.guidance:
• Many targets. Receptors are found in many tissues, so a hormone has many effects, and some of them are indirect, acting through other hormones or the nervous system.
  • Feedback. Giving a hormone suppresses the body’s own production of it (negative feedback). Removing a gland takes away more than one hormone (the adrenal gland has both a cortex and a medulla), and it upsets other axes as well.
  • Dose. Physiological concentrations are tiny (pg to ng per mL), so a dose can easily become pharmacological. Receptors can be up- or down-regulated, and because of carrier proteins, the free and total levels of a hormone differ.
  • Time. Half-lives vary enormously, from minutes for adrenaline to days for thyroxine. Steroids act through gene expression, over hours to days. Release is often pulsatile, and most hormones have a circadian rhythm (ACTH and cortisol peak in the early morning), so the time of day you sample and treat matters, and the season can matter too.
  • Measurement. Handling and blood sampling are stressful in themselves, and they raise cortisol and adrenaline. The assays and the timing of samples matter too, and so does the blood–brain barrier if you want to tell central effects from peripheral ones.
  • Interpretation. Think about controls (vehicle, sham operations), differences between individuals and between species, and ethics.

questions.title: Control of the pituitary
questions.guidance:
• The pituitary has two parts, with different origins, and they’re controlled differently.
  • The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is made of the nerve terminals of neurons whose cell bodies are in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus (the hypothalamic–hypophysial tract). ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin are made in the cell bodies and released from the terminals when action potentials arrive, so it’s controlled by the neurons’ activity. Osmoreceptors drive ADH release, and suckling and stretching of the cervix drive oxytocin release (positive feedback, in the Ferguson reflex).
  • The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) is glandular tissue, controlled by releasing hormones from the hypothalamus (CRH, TRH, GnRH and GHRH) and by inhibiting ones (somatostatin, and dopamine, which inhibits prolactin). These are released into the capillaries of the median eminence and carried down the portal vessels to the trophs of the anterior pituitary.
  • Feedback. The hormones of the peripheral glands (cortisol, thyroid hormones and sex steroids) feed back negatively on the hypothalamus and pituitary in long loops, and there’s short-loop and ultra-short-loop feedback as well.
  • Other influences include circadian rhythms from the SCN (the morning peak of ACTH), stress, pulsatile release and higher brain areas.

questions.title: Addison’s disease and Conn’s syndrome
questions.text: What is Addison’s disease? What is Conn’s syndrome?
questions.guidance:
• Addison’s disease is primary adrenal insufficiency. The adrenal cortex is destroyed, most often by autoimmune disease but also by tuberculosis and other causes, so too little cortisol and aldosterone are made.
  • Its consequences include tiredness, weakness, weight loss, low blood glucose, low blood pressure (especially on standing), low plasma Na⁺ and high plasma K⁺, salt craving, dehydration and darker skin. The skin darkens because low cortisol removes the negative feedback on the pituitary, so ACTH (a POMC derivative) is high. Stress can bring on an adrenal crisis. Addison’s disease is treated by replacing the missing hormones.
  • Conn’s syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism. The zona glomerulosa makes too much aldosterone, whatever the renin–angiotensin system is doing, usually because of an adrenal adenoma.
  • Its consequences are Na⁺ and water retention (which raises blood pressure), loss of K⁺ (low plasma K⁺ causes weakness and cramps), metabolic alkalosis, and suppressed renin (negative feedback). It’s treated with drugs that block mineralocorticoid receptors (spironolactone), or by removing the adenoma.
